prompt.context: QuickEat is a fast food chain in the US with national presence. The CEO of the company is planning to introduce a customer loyalty program called 'Quick Rewards'.
prompt.question: You have been hired as the consultant. Should QuickEat go ahead with the 'Quick Rewards' loyalty program initiative?

clarifying_info.a: A customer gets 2 points for each dollar spent. When a customer reaches 200 points they receive a standard gift. So for each 200 points accumulated, they get one gift.

clarifying_info.q: What does each gift cost the company?
What data do we have on customers and the program's impact?
clarifying_info.a: Data is on a per-store basis. Heavy segment: 8,000 customers per store, 30 avg visits per year, $4.00 avg spend per visit, 20% expected to join the program, 6 avg additional visits per year if they join. Light segment: 12,000 customers per store, 9 avg visits per year, $4.00 avg spend per visit, 5% expected to join, 3 avg additional visits per year if they join. Contribution margin is 20% of revenues.

framework: Step 1: Understand the features of the loyalty program (points structure, reward mechanism)
Step 2: Quantify the incremental revenue benefits — by customer segment
Step 3: Quantify the costs of the program (gift costs based on total points across all spending)
Step 4: Compare incremental profit vs. program costs to determine net profitability
Step 5: Identify any other risks, opportunities, or modifications to improve the program

questions.prompt: Calculate the total revenue without the program for each segment (per store, per year).
questions.guidance: Revenue = # customers × avg visits/year × avg $ per visit. Heavy: 8,000 × 30 × $4 = $960,000. Light: 12,000 × 9 × $4 = $432,000.

math.setup: Revenue = # customers × avg visits per year × avg $ per visit

questions.prompt: Calculate the additional (incremental) revenue generated by the loyalty program for each segment.
questions.guidance: Only the customers who join the program generate additional visits. Additional revenue = (# customers × % joining) × additional visits × avg $ per visit. Heavy: 8,000 × 20% × 6 × $4 = $38,400 (4.0% increase). Light: 12,000 × 5% × 3 × $4 = $7,200 (1.67% increase).

math.setup: Additional revenue = (# customers × % joining program) × additional visits × avg $ per visit
math.answer: Heavy: $38,400 additional revenue (4.00% increase); Light: $7,200 additional revenue (1.67% increase)

questions.prompt: Calculate the incremental income from the program (at 20% contribution margin) for each segment.
Calculate the total cost of gifts for each segment. Note: points are earned on ALL spending, not just incremental spending.
questions.guidance: Key insight: points are earned on total revenue (existing + incremental), not just the additional visits. Total points = total revenue × 2 points per dollar. Gift cost = total points / 200 × $1 per gift. Heavy: total revenue = $960,000 + $38,400 = $998,400 (but the casebook uses total baseline revenue $960,000 for points, yielding 1,920,000 points and $9,600 in gifts). Light: $432,000 + $7,200 = $439,200 (casebook uses $432,000 baseline: 864,000 points, $4,320 in gifts). The cost exceeds the incremental income because rewards are funded by all purchases.

math.setup: Total points = total revenue (all spending by all customers) × 2; Gift cost = total points / 200 × $1
steps: Heavy total revenue (all customers, baseline): 8,000 × 30 × $4 = $960,000; Points = $960,000 × 2 = 1,920,000; Gift cost = 1,920,000 / 200 × $1 = $9,600
Light total revenue (all customers, baseline): 12,000 × 9 × $4 = $432,000; Points = $432,000 × 2 = 864,000; Gift cost = 864,000 / 200 × $1 = $4,320
math.answer: Heavy gift cost: $9,600; Light gift cost: $4,320

questions.prompt: Calculate the net profit (or loss) from the loyalty program for each segment.
questions.guidance: Net profit = incremental income - gift cost. Both segments are unprofitable. The program is a losing proposition because gift costs are spread over all purchases, not just incremental spending.

math.setup: Net profit = incremental income - gift cost
math.answer: Heavy: -$1,920 (loss); Light: -$2,880 (loss). Total net loss = -$4,800 per store.

brainstorming.prompt: The CEO accepts your analysis on the loyalty program. Now he wants advice on other ways to increase sales (ideas apart from the loyalty program). What ideas do you have?

categories.name: New Customers – New Products
ideas: Launch new menu items targeting demographics not currently served
Enter new daypart occasions (e.g., breakfast if not present, late-night)
Create limited-time offerings to attract trial from non-customers
Partner with delivery platforms to reach new audiences with new bundled offerings

categories.name: New Customers – Current Products
ideas: Expand marketing reach and advertising spend to drive trial
Open new store locations or expand into underserved geographies
Offer introductory promotions or free-trial coupons to first-time visitors
Partner with corporates or schools for catering to new customer pools

categories.name: Current Customers – New Products
ideas: Upsell premium or customizable menu items to existing customers
Introduce healthier or dietary-specific options (vegan, gluten-free) to increase wallet share
Launch a mobile app with exclusive menu items or early access

categories.name: Current Customers – Current Products
ideas: Increase visit frequency via targeted promotions or bundled deals
Improve in-store experience and speed to reduce friction and encourage repeat visits
Redesign a revised loyalty program structure that avoids the cost leakage identified (e.g., points only on incremental spend, or co-branded programs with airlines to share costs)
Implement co-branded loyalty programs with airlines or hotels to share costs and broaden appeal
Upsell through combo meal promotions to increase average ticket size

recommendation: Do NOT launch the 'Quick Rewards' program in its current form — it is a net loss of approximately $1,920 for Heavy users and $2,880 for Light users per store, because gift costs are funded by all customer spending rather than just the incremental revenue the program generates.

If the company still wants a loyalty program, it should redesign it: either negotiate lower gift costs with vendors, increase the points threshold required for a gift, restrict the program to Heavy users only (who show higher incremental response), or explore co-branded programs with airlines/hotels to share costs.
risks: The program as designed subsidizes existing behavior — points accrue on purchases customers would have made anyway, making the cost structure fundamentally flawed.
Implementing only for Heavy users may create perceived unfairness among Light users.
Co-branded programs introduce partner dependency and complexity.
Increasing the points threshold may reduce the perceived attractiveness of the program and lower the incremental visit uplift assumed in the model.
next_steps: Model the break-even gift cost and points threshold needed to make the program profitable.
Pilot a redesigned program with Heavy users only in a test market before national rollout.
Explore revenue-growth levers beyond loyalty (new products, new customers, geographic expansion) in parallel.
